sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Git is non-negotiable. Every team uses it. Interviewers assume you know the basics and check with one or two questions. Failing a git question signals you haven't worked in a team environment.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
**Git's three areas:**

```
Working Directory  →(git add)→  Staging Area  →(git commit)→  Local Repo  →(git push)→  Remote Repo
```

`git pull` = `git fetch` + `git merge` (in one step).

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- **The basic workflow** — `git add <file>` → `git commit -m 'message'` → `git push origin branch`.
- **Branching** — `git checkout -b feature/name` creates and switches. `git merge feature/name` merges into current branch.
- **Merge conflict** — two branches changed the same lines. Git marks conflicts with `<<<<<<<` / `=======` / `>>>>>>>`. You resolve manually.
- **`git pull` vs `git fetch`** — fetch downloads remote changes but doesn't merge; pull fetches AND merges.
- **`.gitignore`** — files Git won't track. Always ignore `__pycache__`, `.env`, `venv/`.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **'What is the difference between git pull and git fetch?'** — fetch downloads without merging; pull = fetch + merge.
- **'What is a merge conflict and how do you resolve it?'** — two branches changed the same lines; open the file, pick the correct version, commit.
- **'What does git stash do?'** — temporarily stores uncommitted changes so you can switch branches.
- **'What is the difference between git merge and git rebase?'** — merge preserves history; rebase rewrites it for a linear history.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"My daily Git workflow is: create a feature branch, commit small logical changes with descriptive messages, push to remote, and open a PR for review. For conflicts I open the conflicted file, understand both changes, pick the correct one, and commit the resolution. I always pull before starting new work to avoid diverging from main."*
